patient.name: Maureen Fitzgerald
patient.complaint: Swollen legs, a bloated tummy and tiredness for 4 months
background: COPD with pulmonary hypertension; ex-smoker of 40 pack-years

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely heart valve abnormality?' from a murmur that is louder on inspiration, often in an injector with fever (TR) or a child with Noonan features (pulmonary stenosis).

points: Maureen, 68: **ankle swelling** and abdominal bloating for 4 months.
Breathless and exhausted walking up her stairs.
Dull ache under her right ribs.

steps.lead: Maureen's problem is on the **right side** of the heart: a leaking tricuspid valve impairing right-sided flow.
Maureen's **pulmonary hypertension** is her key risk factor. Others are IV drug use, congenital and rheumatic disease.

points: **Pansystolic murmur** at the lower left sternal edge.
JVP raised to the earlobe with **giant V waves**.
Left parasternal heave; liver pulsates under the hand.

steps.q: A pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, louder on inspiration. Which lesion?
steps.r: **Tricuspid regurgitation**: lower left sternal edge, louder on inspiration (**Carvallo's sign**). MR is at the apex and louder on expiration.

steps.lead: Maureen has classic **TR**: the commonest right-sided lesion. The notes compare it with the other three right-sided lesions.

steps.text: All right-sided murmurs get **louder on inspiration**; left-sided murmurs get louder on **expiration**.

visual.title: Where Maureen's liver pulsates
visual.caption: **Pulsatile hepatomegaly**: each systole, TR pushes blood back into the hepatic veins.

steps.lead: Maureen's TR is functional. A young injector with fever would point to **tricuspid endocarditis**; a child with Noonan to **pulmonary stenosis**.
Maureen already has **right heart failure** and an irregular pulse: both complications of TR.

steps.text: Pulmonary stenosis vs aortic stenosis: PS presents in **childhood**, sits at the upper left sternal edge, radiates to the **shoulder** not the carotids, and has a large A wave.

investigation.exam: Expect echocardiography as the test that confirms the lesion, with ECG and chest X-ray as supporting tests.

steps.r: **Echocardiography** is the gold standard: it shows the leak, its severity and the cause.

steps.lead: Maureen's **echo** shows severe TR through a stretched annulus, a dilated right ventricle and raised pulmonary pressure.

steps.title: Maureen's echo and bloods
steps.text: Normal LV but a big RV and high pulmonary pressure: functional TR. Liver tests are up from congestion.

visual.title: Maureen's PA systolic pressure
visual.label: Maureen 62
visual.caption: Pulmonary hypertension raises RV afterload, dilates the RV and stretches the tricuspid annulus.

steps.lead: Maureen's **ECG** and **chest X-ray** support the picture: an arrhythmia and an enlarged heart.

visual.title: Maureen's ECG
visual.caption: **Atrial fibrillation**: her right atrium is dilated by the regurgitant jet.

visual.title: Maureen's chest X-ray
visual.caption: Enlarged heart (big right atrium) and a small right pleural effusion.

steps.text: ECG and CXR cannot grade a valve. The 'confirm' or 'gold standard' answer for any valve lesion is **echocardiography**.

management.exam: Expect 'treat the cause' (infection, pulmonary hypertension), furosemide for fluid overload, and surgical repair or replacement for severe disease.

steps.lead: For Maureen, **treating the cause** means treating her pulmonary hypertension, and **furosemide** clears her fluid.

steps.text: In COPD with cor pulmonale and low oxygen, **long-term oxygen therapy** is how UK practice treats the cause (NICE), after formal blood gas assessment.

steps.q: Maureen is fluid overloaded with severe functional TR. What eases her swelling first?
steps.r: A loop diuretic, **furosemide**, relieves fluid overload. Surgery is for severe disease that fails treatment.

visual.title: Maureen's weight on furosemide
visual.caption: Nearly 5 kg of fluid lost; check renal function and potassium daily.

steps.lead: If Maureen's severe TR stays symptomatic despite treatment, she would be considered for **surgical valve repair or replacement**.

steps.title: Right heart valve disease pathway
nodes: Treat the cause: pulmonary hypertension, infection
Rate control and anticoagulation if AF
Severe, symptomatic: surgical repair or replacement

steps.lead: Maureen's plan follows **ESC/BSE valvular guidance**: confirm on echo, treat the cause, diurese, and refer severe disease for surgery.

steps.text: Do not reach for valve surgery first in **functional TR**. The leak is driven by pulmonary hypertension; fix the driver and the fluid first.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanisms: Carvallo's sign, giant V waves, pulsatile liver, functional TR from pulmonary hypertension, and why IVDU affects the tricuspid valve.

steps.lead: Each systole, blood leaks back into Maureen's right atrium, pushing up her JVP as a **giant V wave**.
That back pressure reaches Maureen's liver: it **pulsates**, and long-standing congestion can cause **cardiac cirrhosis**.

steps.title: From lungs to liver
nodes: RA pressure rises: giant V waves
Hepatic congestion: pulsatile liver, cardiac cirrhosis

steps.lead: Maureen's high **RV afterload** dilated her right ventricle and pulled the valve leaflets apart.
On inspiration, Maureen's falling chest pressure pulls more blood into the right heart, so her murmur gets louder: **Carvallo's sign**.

steps.q: Why does Maureen's murmur get louder when she breathes in?
o: Increased venous return to the right heart
steps.r: Negative intrathoracic pressure on inspiration increases **venous return** and flow across the right-sided valve.

steps.lead: An injector's organisms reach the **right heart first** via the veins, which is why tricuspid endocarditis follows IV drug use.
Congenital pulmonary stenosis is a **fixed** RV outflow obstruction, giving a crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur.

mcq.q: What is the most common right-sided valve lesion?
mcq.r: **Tricuspid regurgitation**, often secondary to pulmonary hypertension.

Which liver sign is typical of severe TR?
mcq.r: **Pulsatile hepatomegaly** from systolic backflow into the hepatic veins.

mcq.q: Which drug treats fluid overload in TR?
Definitive treatment for severe right-sided valve disease?
How does pulmonary hypertension cause TR?
mcq.r: Raised RV afterload dilates the RV and **stretches the annulus**: functional TR.

glossary.Tricuspid regurgitation: Leak of blood from the right ventricle back into the right atrium in systole.
glossary.Tricuspid stenosis: Narrowed tricuspid valve, usually rheumatic, giving a mid-diastolic murmur.
glossary.Pulmonary stenosis: Narrowed pulmonary valve obstructing right ventricular outflow; usually congenital.
glossary.Pulmonary regurgitation: Leak of blood from the pulmonary artery back into the right ventricle in diastole.
glossary.Carvallo's sign: A right-sided murmur that gets louder on inspiration.
glossary.V wave: JVP wave from right atrial filling in systole; giant in tricuspid regurgitation.
glossary.C-V wave: A merged, giant systolic wave in the JVP seen in tricuspid regurgitation.
glossary.A wave: JVP wave from right atrial contraction; large in pulmonary stenosis.
glossary.JVP: Jugular venous pressure: the venous pulse in the neck, reflecting right atrial pressure.
glossary.Parasternal heave: A lifting impulse beside the sternum from an enlarged right ventricle.
glossary.Pulsatile hepatomegaly: An enlarged liver that pulses with each heartbeat, typical of severe TR.
glossary.Cardiac cirrhosis: Liver scarring from long-term venous congestion in right heart failure.
glossary.Functional TR: TR from a dilated right ventricle stretching a structurally normal valve.
glossary.Annulus: The fibrous ring that supports a heart valve.
glossary.Afterload: The resistance the ventricle must pump against.
glossary.Pulmonary hypertension: Raised blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries.
glossary.Cor pulmonale: Right heart failure caused by lung disease and pulmonary hypertension.
glossary.Right heart failure: Failure of the right ventricle causing raised JVP, oedema, ascites and hepatomegaly.
glossary.Noonan syndrome: Genetic syndrome with short stature, webbed neck and pulmonary valve stenosis.
glossary.Ejection systolic murmur: Crescendo-decrescendo murmur in mid-systole, as in aortic or pulmonary stenosis.
glossary.Crescendo-decrescendo: A murmur that builds up then fades, typical of outflow obstruction.
glossary.Pansystolic murmur: A murmur that lasts throughout systole, as in TR or MR.
glossary.Mid-diastolic murmur: A murmur in mid-diastole, as in tricuspid or mitral stenosis.
glossary.Early diastolic murmur: A murmur straight after S2, as in pulmonary or aortic regurgitation.
glossary.Thrill: A palpable murmur felt as a vibration.
glossary.Echocardiogram: Ultrasound of the heart; the gold standard for valve disease.
glossary.Furosemide: Loop diuretic that removes excess fluid.
glossary.Infective endocarditis: Infection of a heart valve forming vegetations.
glossary.Hepatojugular reflux: A sustained rise in JVP when the liver is pressed.
glossary.Long-term oxygen therapy: Home oxygen for at least 15 hours a day for chronic hypoxaemia, e.g. COPD with cor pulmonale.
glossary.AF: Atrial fibrillation: chaotic atrial activity with an irregularly irregular pulse.

technique.stem: A 63 year old man with pulmonary hypertension has 3 months of leg swelling and right upper abdominal discomfort. His pulse rate is 90 bpm, BP 122/74 mmHg. His JVP is raised with a large systolic wave. There is a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that increases on inspiration.
technique.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on abdominal examination?

steps.x: Finding on examination: link the valve lesion to the abdomen.
PH, giant V waves, pansystolic murmur louder on inspiration: severe TR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe TR transmits systolic pressure to the hepatic veins: **pulsatile hepatomegaly**.

elim: Caput medusae is portal hypertension from cirrhosis.
A palpable gallbladder with jaundice suggests pancreatic cancer.
Isolated splenomegaly suggests portal hypertension or haematological disease.
Visible peristalsis is bowel obstruction.

steps.x: **C.** Giant V waves + TR = pulsatile liver.

technique.stem: A 58 year old woman has breathlessness and ankle swelling. There is a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that is louder on inspiration, and giant V waves in the JVP. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. ECG shows sinus rhythm with right axis deviation.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

clues: pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Invasive and not needed to confirm TR.
CXR supports but cannot show the valve.
CTPA looks for PE.
BNP indicates heart strain but not which valve.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man with severe COPD has ankle oedema, a raised JVP and functional tricuspid regurgitation on echo, with an estimated pulmonary artery pressure of 58 mmHg. On two arterial blood gases 3 weeks apart while stable, his PaO2 is 7.1 kPa breathing air. He stopped smoking 5 years ago. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment of the underlying cause of his valve disease?

steps.x: It asks for treatment of the underlying CAUSE, not the valve.
Hypoxic COPD causes pulmonary hypertension, which drives functional TR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Long-term oxygen therapy** (PaO2 below 7.3 kPa, non-smoker) treats the hypoxic pulmonary hypertension.

elim: Beta-blockers do not treat pulmonary hypertension.
Steroids are for exacerbations, not long-term PH.
Pericardiectomy is for constrictive pericarditis.
Surgery is for severe disease failing treatment; it does not fix the cause.

technique.stem: A 55 year old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension has developed tricuspid regurgitation. Echo shows structurally normal tricuspid leaflets, a dilated right ventricle and a dilated tricuspid annulus.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her regurgitation?
o: Right ventricular dilation stretching the annulus

steps.x: Mechanism: why is a normal valve leaking?
Normal leaflets, big RV, big annulus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Raised RV afterload dilates the RV and **stretches the annulus**: functional TR.

elim: No infection; leaflets are normal.
Rheumatic disease thickens and fuses leaflets.
Myxomatous leaflets would be abnormal on echo.
No shunt is described.

steps.x: **D.** PH → RV dilation → annular stretch → functional TR.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman with long-standing left heart failure has increasing ankle swelling and abdominal distension. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 112/70 mmHg. Her JVP is raised with prominent systolic waves. There is a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that is louder on inspiration, and a left parasternal heave.
practice.q: Which is the most likely heart valve abnormality?
practice.e: A pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, louder on inspiration, with prominent V waves and a parasternal heave is tricuspid regurgitation, here secondary to left heart failure.

clues: pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: AS is ejection systolic to the carotids.
MR is at the apex to the axilla, louder on expiration.
PS is ejection systolic at the upper left sternal edge.
TS is mid-diastolic.

practice.stem: An 8 year old boy has exertional breathlessness and fainted once while playing football. He is short with a webbed neck and low-set ears. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 100/64 mmHg. There is an ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge radiating to the left shoulder, with a palpable thrill. His JVP shows a large A wave.
practice.q: Which is the most likely heart valve abnormality?
practice.e: A child with Noonan features, an ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge radiating to the shoulder, a thrill and a large A wave has congenital pulmonary stenosis.

steps.x: Valve abnormality in a child: read the syndrome and the murmur.
Noonan features + ESM upper left sternal edge to shoulder + large A wave.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: AS radiates to the carotids, without a large A wave.
ASD gives fixed splitting of S2.
Coarctation gives radio-femoral delay and upper limb hypertension.
VSD is pansystolic at the lower left sternal edge.

steps.x: **D.** Noonan + ESM to shoulder = pulmonary stenosis.

practice.stem: A 31 year old man who injects heroin has a 10 day history of fever and rigors. His temperature is 39.3°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 108/68 mmHg. There is a new murmur at the lower left sternal edge that is louder on inspiration.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his murmur?
practice.e: Fever, IV drug use and a new right-sided murmur louder on inspiration is tricuspid regurgitation from right-sided Staph. aureus endocarditis.

steps.x: Cause of a murmur in a febrile injector.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: AR is early diastolic, left-sided.
AS is ejection systolic to the carotids.
MR is at the apex, louder on expiration.
MVP gives a click and late systolic murmur at the apex.

steps.x: **E.** IVDU + fever + new murmur = TR (right-sided IE).

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman has tricuspid regurgitation secondary to pulmonary hypertension. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. She is sitting at 45 degrees and her JVP is raised.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding in her JVP waveform?
practice.e: In TR, systolic backflow into the right atrium gives prominent (giant) V or C-V waves.

steps.x: JVP waveform in a named lesion.
TR = systolic backflow into the RA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Absent A waves mean AF.
Cannon A waves are complete heart block.
Large A waves are pulmonary stenosis or pulmonary hypertension without TR.
A slow Y descent is tricuspid stenosis.

practice.stem: A 69 year old woman with COPD has severe tricuspid regurgitation. Echo shows structurally normal leaflets, a dilated right ventricle and an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 64 mmHg. Left heart function is normal. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her tricuspid regurgitation?
practice.e: Normal leaflets with RV dilation and a high pulmonary pressure means functional TR secondary to pulmonary hypertension, here from COPD.

steps.x: Cause of TR: primary leaflet disease or secondary?
Normal leaflets + PH + COPD: secondary (functional) TR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Carcinoid thickens and fixes the leaflets.
Ebstein's is a congenital displaced valve, seen as abnormal leaflets.
Endocarditis needs fever and gives vegetations.
Rheumatic disease thickens leaflets and causes stenosis.

steps.x: **D.** TR is often secondary to pulmonary hypertension.

practice.stem: A 49 year old woman had rheumatic fever as a child. She has fatigue, ankle swelling and abdominal swelling. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg. Her JVP is raised. There is a low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that is louder on inspiration.
practice.q: Which is the most likely heart valve abnormality?
practice.e: A mid-diastolic murmur at the lower sternal edge, louder on inspiration, with a raised JVP after rheumatic fever is tricuspid stenosis. Mitral stenosis is heard at the apex and louder in expiration.

clues: mid-diastolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: AR is early diastolic and louder in expiration.
MS is at the apex, louder in expiration.
PR is early diastolic at the pulmonary area.
TR is pansystolic, not diastolic.

practice.stem: A 6 year old girl with Noonan syndrome has an ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge with a thrill. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. Her ECG shows right ventricular hypertrophy.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
practice.e: Echocardiography is the gold standard: it shows the abnormal pulmonary valve and the pressure gradient across it.

clues: left upper sternal edge with a thrill

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: MRI is not first-line for valve diagnosis.
CXR may show post-stenotic dilation but cannot confirm.
Exercise testing is unsafe and does not image the valve.
Genetic testing confirms Noonan, not the valve lesion.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man with known severe tricuspid regurgitation has 2 days of palpitations. His pulse rate is 132 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 116/72 mmHg. He is not breathless at rest and has no chest pain.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: A 12-lead ECG is the first test for palpitations and an irregular pulse; TR dilates the right atrium and predisposes to arrhythmias such as AF.

steps.x: Initial investigation for a symptom in known TR.
Irregular pulse in a dilated right atrium: arrhythmia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Ambulatory ECG is for intermittent symptoms, not an arrhythmia present now.
MRI is not an initial test.
No hypoxia or pleuritic pain to suggest PE.
The valve is already known; the rhythm is the question.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman has functional tricuspid regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension. She has gained 4 kg in 2 weeks with pitting oedema to the knees and ascites. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Renal function is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of her symptoms?
practice.e: A loop diuretic such as furosemide relieves fluid overload in right heart valve disease. Surgery is for severe disease that fails treatment.

steps.x: Symptom management: what is the problem?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Amlodipine worsens ankle oedema.
No AF to rate-control.
Surgery is not the first step for functional TR.
No AF or clot to anticoagulate.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman who injects drugs has a new pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. Three sets of blood cultures grow meticillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and echo shows a tricuspid valve vegetation. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. She has no allergies.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment of the underlying cause?
practice.e: Her TR is caused by MSSA endocarditis, so treat the infection: high-dose IV flucloxacillin for weeks. Surgery is for failure, abscess or instability.

steps.x: Treat the cause of right-sided valve disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Furosemide does not treat infection.
Oral amoxicillin does not cover Staph. aureus endocarditis.
She is stable; antibiotics come first.
Anticoagulation is not indicated and risks bleeding from septic emboli.

practice.stem: A 57 year old man had tricuspid valve endocarditis 2 years ago, cured with antibiotics. He now has severe primary tricuspid regurgitation with a flail leaflet. Despite maximal diuretics he has worsening oedema, ascites and breathlessness. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Left heart function is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Surgical tricuspid valve repair or replacement
practice.e: Severe, symptomatic TR that fails medical therapy needs surgical valve repair or replacement.

steps.x: Next step when medical treatment has failed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Diuretics are already maximal.
No hypoxia; oxygen will not fix a flail leaflet.
Pericardiectomy treats constrictive pericarditis.
Symptoms are worsening; waiting is unsafe.

practice.stem: A 60 year old woman has a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. The murmur becomes louder when she takes a deep breath in and quieter on expiration.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the change in murmur intensity?
o: Decreased left ventricular afterload on inspiration
Increased left atrial filling on inspiration
Increased venous return to the right heart on inspiration
Reduced right ventricular preload on inspiration
practice.e: Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, increasing venous return to the right heart and flow across the diseased tricuspid valve (Carvallo's sign).

clues: louder when she takes a deep breath in
steps.x: Right-sided murmur louder on inspiration: Carvallo's sign.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Increased venous return** to the right heart.

elim: LV afterload changes affect left-sided murmurs.
Left atrial filling falls slightly on inspiration.
Heart rate rises slightly on inspiration (sinus arrhythmia).
RV preload increases, not falls.

steps.x: **C.** Inspiration → more venous return → louder right-sided murmur.
